title: The boy and the crocodile
hook: a boy in the river, a crocodile on his leg, and the one thing he asks his mother for
carry: a human birth: the rare chance to be free
tomorrow: Fear not, there is a way

segments.voice: Yesterday: Narada's water, and maya, real while it lasts. Today, back to the boy who would become Advaita's great teacher.

A boy in Kerala, about eight years old by tradition, wants one thing: to become a monk. His father has died, and his mother, Aryamba, won't hear of it. He's all she has. Then one day he's bathing in the river near home, and a crocodile clamps onto his leg and starts dragging him under. His mother runs to the bank. And from the water the boy calls out: let me take the vows now, so at least I die a monk.
screen: `A BOY WHO WANTS TO BE A MONK.` → `A CROCODILE IN THE RIVER.` → `LET ME TAKE THE VOWS.`

segments.voice: She says yes. And the story says, at that moment, the crocodile lets go. That boy is Shankara, as his tradition tells it. He promises his mother he'll come back whenever she needs him, and tradition says he kept that promise. Then he walks north, hundreds of miles, looking for a teacher, and finds one on the banks of the Narmada: Govinda. Why tell this story now? Because a book of Shankara's school, the Vivekachudamani, the crest-jewel of discernment, opens with exactly what that boy had. Tradition says Shankara wrote it; many modern scholars think a later teacher of his school did. Paraphrased, it says: three things are rare, and come only by grace. Being human. Longing for freedom. And the company of a great soul. Here's the Hindu teaching underneath. In the Hindu picture of many lives, a soul passes through many kinds of bodies, and a human birth is rare. Animals have a self too, the same atman. But a human life is the one where you can ask who am I, and seek moksha, freedom. That's why Hindu elders say: don't waste it. Then the longing, mumukshutva: the boy in the river. Then a teacher. And today? Most of us aren't monks, and no one needs a crocodile. But when the weeks blur into errands and scrolling, the elders' line lands: this is the one kind of life that can ask who am I. Spend a little of it on that question, and be grateful for whoever pointed you to it.
screen: `THE CROCODILE LETS GO.` · `THE CREST-JEWEL OF DISCERNMENT.` · `BEING HUMAN. LONGING. A GREAT SOUL.` · `A HUMAN LIFE: THE CHANCE FOR MOKSHA.` · then, large: `THE RARE CHANCE.`

segments.voice: Count your own three rare things: that you're here, a human being, breathing, able to wonder; that some part of you longs for something more, or you wouldn't be listening; and the people who pointed you here, a teacher, a parent, a friend, a book. Bring one of them to mind. If you pray, you can give thanks for them; if not, just hold them for a breath or two.
Advaita, through the Vivekachudamani's opening: three rare things, a human birth, the longing for freedom, and a great soul's company.
Your line: a human birth is the rare chance to be free. Day two eighty-four, done.

screen: `DAY 284 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: FEAR NOT, THERE IS A WAY.`

howItsDone: The Vivekachudamani is studied and chanted in Advaita circles as an introduction to the whole teaching; its opening verses on the rarity of human birth, the longing for freedom and the company of the wise are often recited on their own.

chat.meaning: The Vivekachudamani counts a human birth first among three rare things. Every being has a self, but a human life is the chance to seek freedom, like the boy Shankara longing for it in the river.
